claims.text: The starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a solid-solution state.
Substitution with elements having different atomic radii introduces or increases lattice distortion.
Some Co can be replaced by Cu as a means of introducing lattice distortion.
Some Cr can be replaced by Mn as a means of introducing lattice distortion.
Increased lattice distortion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Substitution-induced lattice distortion changes dislocation mobility.
Substitution-induced lattice distortion changes grain-boundary cohesion.
The proposed substitution promotes dislocation activity.
The proposed substitution promotes grain-boundary sliding.
Promoted dislocation activity and grain-boundary sliding maintain or improve plasticity.
The substitutionally modified alloy will have greater hardness than the starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
The substitutionally modified alloy will have greater strength than the starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy at both 25 °C and 600 °C.
The substitutionally modified alloy will maintain or increase plastic strain relative to the starting alloy.
The proposed comparison uses uniaxial compression at 25 °C and 600 °C and strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1.
The baseline CoCrFeNiTi alloy is without lattice distortion.

contradictions.description: Replacing Co with Cu or Cr with Mn changes the nominal element set, whereas the boundary states that the hypothesis is restricted to the CoCrFeNiTi material system.

The baseline is described categorically as being 'without lattice distortion,' while the intervention is framed as introducing lattice distortion rather than increasing or modifying it; this is not reconciled with the baseline being a multicomponent CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
